content: Being overweight or obese significantly increases the likelihood of developing cancer. The risk of cancer rises proportionally with the amount of excess weight a person gains and the duration for which they remain overweight. It may be surprising to learn that being overweight or obese is associated with an increased risk of developing 13 specific types of cancer. These cancers collectively account for 40% of all cancer diagnoses in the United States annually. While many factors contribute to cancer risk, avoiding tobacco use and maintaining a healthy weight are two of the most effective strategies to reduce the likelihood of developing cancer. It is important to note that being overweight or obese does not guarantee that an individual will develop cancer, but it does increase their risk compared to individuals with a healthy weight. Cancers Associated with Obesity Excess weight or obesity is linked to a higher risk of developing the following 13 types of cancer: Adenocarcinoma of the esophagus Breast cancer (in postmenopausal women) Colorectal cancer Uterine cancer Gallbladder cancer Cancer of the upper stomach Kidney cancer Liver cancer Ovarian cancer Pancreatic cancer Thyroid cancer Meningioma (a type of brain tumor) Multiple myeloma Defining Overweight and Obesity Overweight and obesity are defined as body weight that exceeds what is considered healthy for a given height. Body mass index (BMI) is commonly used as a screening tool to classify individuals as overweight or obese. For adults: A BMI between 25.0 and 29.9 is classified as overweight. A BMI of 30.0 or higher is classified as obesity. For children and adolescents, BMI is calculated similarly but interpreted differently, as it is compared to the average BMI of peers in the same age group. Mechanisms Linking Obesity to Cancer Excess weight and obesity can induce physiological changes in the body, including chronic inflammation, elevated levels of insulin and insulin-like growth factors, and increased concentrations of sex hormones. These alterations can contribute to the development of cancer. The risk of cancer increases with the amount of excess weight gained and the duration of being overweight. Strategies to Reduce Cancer Risk Adopting a healthy lifestyle can help achieve and maintain a healthy weight, thereby reducing the risk of obesity-related cancers. This includes following a nutritious eating plan and engaging in regular physical activity. Support for Cancer Survivors Programs such as Talk to Someone: Physical Activity and Nutrition provide practical advice for cancer survivors to improve their physical activity levels and dietary habits. Role of Healthcare Providers Healthcare professionals play a critical role in helping patients maintain a healthy weight. They can: Measure patients' weight, height, and BMI. Educate patients about the link between healthy weight and reduced cancer risk. Connect patients and their families with community resources that promote access to healthy food and physical activity. Encourage adult patients to participate in behavioral interventions recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. These interventions aim to help patients lose at least 5% of their body weight through dietary modifications and increased physical activity. Screen children and adolescents aged 6 years or older for obesity and, if necessary, refer them to behavioral interventions to support weight loss. Prevalence of Obesity and Related Cancers Obesity is highly prevalent in the United States. Recent data indicate that approximately 42% of adults and 20% of children and adolescents are classified as obese. Adults with obesity face a higher risk of numerous serious health conditions, including cancer, compared to individuals with a healthy weight. Between 2005 and 2014, the incidence of cancers associated with overweight and obesity increased in the United States, while the incidence of cancers linked to other factors declined. During this period: The rate of new obesity-related cancers (excluding colorectal cancer) rose by 7%. The rate of new cancers unrelated to obesity decreased by 13%. The incidence of colorectal cancer dropped by 23%, likely due to the effectiveness of screening tests in preventing this type of cancer. Each year, more than 684,000 cases of obesity-associated cancers are diagnosed in the United States, including over 210,000 cases in men and 470,000 cases in women. Among women, postmenopausal breast cancer is the most common obesity-related cancer, while colorectal cancer is the most common among men. Over 90% of new obesity-related cancer cases occur in individuals aged 50 or older.
